title: The Parts of Yourself You Were Taught to Hide

reels.hook: As a child, what wasn't it safe to be?
reels.hook_b: Every child learns which parts of them are welcome.
cards: As a child, what wasn't it safe to be?
Too loud. Too sad. Too needy. Too soft.
Those parts didn't disappear. They went underground.
People think about their secrets far more alone than they hide them in company.
Hiding costs most at 3 a.m., not at dinner.
Save this. Write your list tonight.
reels.visual: V3 still of a closed door with light under it (tag door-light), else V1 + grain.
reels.caption:
Every child learns which parts of them are welcome and which bring trouble. The rest go underground.

In ten studies on secrets, people spent far more time thinking about what they hid when they were alone than actually hiding it in conversation. It was the mind-wandering, not the hiding, that went with lower wellbeing.

As a child, what wasn't it safe to be?

Evidence: Slepian, Chun & Mason (2017). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
reels.first_comment: One word: what wasn't it safe to be?

reels.hook: You learned to make a joke instead of crying.
reels.hook_b: The sensitive boy learns to make a joke instead.
cards: You learned to make a joke instead of crying.
It worked. It kept you safe.
But self-reliance norms were linked to worse mental health and less help-seeking.
Meta-analysis: Wong et al., J. Counseling Psychology (2017)
Hiding a feeling isn't strength. Choosing when to show it is.
Send this to the funniest person you know.

source.author: Wong, Ho, Wang & Miller
source.work: Masculine norms and mental health (J. Counseling Psychology 64(1))

reels.caption:
Plenty of men learned early that some feelings were welcome and some weren't. The joke, the change of subject, the sudden helpfulness: they arrive exactly when a feeling would have.

In meta-analyses, conforming to traditional masculine norms, self-reliance especially, was linked to worse mental health and less help-seeking.

Strength isn't hiding a feeling. It's being able to choose when to show it.

What do you make a joke about instead?

Evidence: Wong et al. (2017). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.

carousel_caption:
Every child runs the same quiet experiment: show a feeling, watch the adults' faces, learn what's welcome.

The unwelcome parts don't vanish. Research on suppression and on secrets suggests carrying them costs most when we're alone with them.

Which part would you like back?

Evidence: Gross & John 2003; Slepian, Chun & Mason 2017; Tangney & Dearing 2002. Frameworks: Jung (persona, shadow), Winnicott (true and false self), interpretive, not tested therapies.
notes: In ten studies on secrets, people spent much more time thinking about what they were hiding when they were alone than actually hiding it from someone. And the thinking, not the hiding, went with lower wellbeing. Hiding costs most at 3 a.m.

Winnicott described a 'false self' a child builds to fit what the people around them need, protecting a true self that doesn't feel safe to show. He didn't see it as a failure. It's a good adaptation. It only becomes a problem when it's all there is.
Finish this sentence five times tonight: 'As a child, it wasn't safe to be…' Then ask which of those you'd like back. This week's essay is about the parts that went underground.
